slides.text:
A function can call itself. Each call gets its own copy of the parameters and works on a smaller version of the problem, until a case so small it needs no more calls. You will count down, multiply, add and trace what runs when, then make two functions call each other and carry a result in a parameter.

The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
solve(problem):
    if the problem is tiny:
        give the answer
    otherwise:
        solve(a smaller problem)

slides.text:
A recursive function has two parts. The **base case** stops the calls and answers directly. The **recursive case** calls the same function with a smaller input.

The snippet is pseudo code.
Without a base case the calls never stop. The input must also get closer to the base case with every call, or the function runs forever.

slides.text:
Code placed **before** the recursive call runs on the way in. Code placed **after** it waits, and runs on the way back out, once the deeper call has finished.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
f(n):
    if n > 0:
        before(n)
        f(n - 1)
        after(n)

slides.text: A function can also call itself **twice**. Each of those calls makes two more, so the number of calls grows quickly. The answer still comes from the same two parts: a base case, and the results of the smaller calls combined.

slides.text:
Two functions can call each other. `a` calls `b` and `b` calls `a`, until one of them reaches a base case. Go lets you declare functions in any order, so neither has to come first.

The snippet is pseudo code.
slides.code:
a(n):
    if n is tiny: answer
    otherwise: b(n - 1)

b(n):
    if n is tiny: answer
    otherwise: a(n - 1)

slides.text:
A parameter can carry the work done so far. This **accumulator** starts at a known value, grows with every call, and the base case returns it. A small entry function often starts it, so callers do not have to.

The snippet is pseudo code.

A recursive function can return several values, like any function. Each call gets a pair from the smaller call and builds its own pair from it.

A function with no base case, or one that never reaches it, keeps calling until the program crashes with a stack overflow. Go stops it for you, but the output is an error, not a result.
